summary: Defines the INFO method for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), which lets endpoints send application-level information during an existing session, along with an Info Package mechanism for defining what such messages carry. It also keeps a legacy mode compatible with earlier use. It is a proposed standard and obsoletes RFC 2976.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP is the protocol that sets up and controls a call. This RFC adds a way to pass extra application data during a call, and a naming scheme so that both ends agree on what that data is. Without the naming, every use of the data had to be configured by hand, which led to devices that did not understand each other.

subtitle: SIP gets a method for passing application data inside a call, plus a labelling scheme so both ends know what the data means.

tldr.problem: Applications running inside a SIP session, such as telephony signalling carried in message bodies, need to exchange data during the call. Earlier versions of the INFO method left every such use to be configured by hand, with no way for the two ends to say what they understood, which caused interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the INFO method and an Info Package mechanism. Each kind of application data is described in an Info Package with a name, and the Recv-Info header field says which packages a user agent will accept while the Info-Package header field says which one a given request carries.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6086 is a Proposed Standard from January 2011 that obsoletes RFC 2976. A legacy mode of use is kept for backward compatibility, new usages must use the Info Package mechanism, and the response code 469 was registered to report a request for a package the receiver does not accept.

today: RFC 6086 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2011. It obsoletes RFC 2976, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Legacy INFO usage is kept for backward compatibility, but the RFC requires any new use of the method to be defined as an Info Package.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines a method, INFO, for the Session Initiation Protocol, RFC 3261. The purpose of the INFO message is to carry application level information between endpoints, using the SIP dialog signaling path. The INFO method is not used to update characteristics of a SIP dialog or session; it allows the applications that use the session to exchange information, which might update the state of those applications.

Use of the INFO method does not constitute a separate dialog usage. INFO messages are always part of, and share the fate of, an invite dialog usage, as described in RFC 5057. They cannot be sent as part of other dialog usages, or outside an existing dialog.

The document also defines an Info Package mechanism. An Info Package specification defines the content and semantics of the information carried in an INFO message associated with that package, and the mechanism gives user agents a way to say which Info Packages they are willing to receive INFO requests for, and which package a specific INFO request belongs to.

A user agent uses the Recv-Info header field, on a per-dialog basis, to indicate for which Info Packages it is willing to receive INFO requests. It can indicate an initial set during dialog establishment and a new set during the lifetime of the invite dialog usage. An empty Recv-Info header field, that is, a header field without a value, means the agent is not willing to receive INFO requests for any Info Package while still informing other agents that it supports the mechanism. When a user agent sends an INFO request, it uses the Info-Package header field to say which package the request is associated with, and one particular INFO request can only be associated with a single Info Package.
sections.plainLanguage: The method carries application data along the signaling path of a call that already exists. Two header fields do the labelling: one says what the receiver is willing to accept, the other says what a particular message contains.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
A number of applications, standardized and proprietary, made use of the INFO method as it was defined in RFC 2976, called legacy INFO usage in this document. RFC 3372 specifies the encapsulation of ISDN User Part in SIP message bodies, and the ITU-T and the Third Generation Partnership Project have specified similar procedures. ECMA-355 specifies the encapsulation of QSIG in SIP message bodies. RFC 5022 specifies how INFO is used as a transport mechanism by the Media Server Control Markup Language, which uses an option-tag in the Require header field to ensure the receiver understands the INFO content, and RFC 5707 does the same for the Media Server Markup Language. Companies have also used INFO messages to request fast video update, for which a standardized mechanism based on RTCP now exists in RFC 5168, and to transport Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency tones, for which all mechanisms are proprietary and have not been standardized.

RFC 2976 did not define mechanisms that would let a user agent indicate the types of applications and contexts in which it supports the INFO method, or the types of applications and contexts with which a specific INFO message is associated. Because legacy INFO usages have no associated Info Packages, it is not possible to use the Recv-Info and Info-Package header fields with them: a user agent cannot use Recv-Info to say which legacy usages it will accept, and cannot use Info-Package to say which legacy usage a request belongs to.

Legacy usages therefore often require static configuration of the types of applications and contexts for which the agents support INFO and the way they handle application information carried in it. This has caused interoperability problems in the industry. To overcome these problems, the SIP Working Group spent years reaching agreement on whether it was more appropriate to fix INFO by defining a registration mechanism for the ways it was used, or to deprecate it altogether. The eventual direction was to publish a framework for the registration of Info Packages.
sections.plainLanguage: Several unrelated uses of the same method had grown up, and nothing recorded what any of them meant. Two devices could both follow the rules and still disagree about what a message contained. The fix is a registry of named uses, so that the meaning is written down somewhere both ends can point to.

sections.title: The INFO Method
sections.content:
An INFO request can be associated with an Info Package or with a legacy INFO usage. Its construction is the same as any other non-target refresh request within an existing invite dialog usage, as described in Section 12.2 of RFC 3261. When a user agent sends an INFO request associated with an Info Package, it MUST include an Info-Package header field saying which package the request is associated with, and a specific request can be used for only a single package. When the request is associated with a legacy usage, there is no package and the agent MUST NOT include the Info-Package header field. The INFO request MUST NOT contain a Recv-Info header field.

A user agent MUST NOT send an INFO request outside an invite dialog usage, and MUST NOT send a request for an Info Package inside an invite dialog usage if the remote agent has not indicated willingness to receive that package within that dialog. If a user agent receives a 469 response to an INFO request, the response represents a Transaction Only failure, and the agent MUST NOT terminate the invite dialog usage. Because of the possibility of forking, the agent that sends the initial INVITE request MUST be prepared to receive INFO requests from multiple remote agents during the early dialog phase, and MUST be prepared to receive different Recv-Info header field values from different remote agents.

On the receiving side, if a user agent receives an INFO request associated with an Info Package that it has not said it will accept, it MUST send a 469 response, which contains a Recv-Info header field with the packages it is willing to receive. The agent MUST NOT use that response to update the set of packages; it only indicates the current set. If the request is associated with a package and the body part with Content-Disposition Info-Package has a MIME type that the agent supports but not in the context of that package, it is RECOMMENDED that the agent send a 415 response. The agent MAY send other error responses, such as 4xx, 5xx and 6xx, in accordance with the error-handling procedures of RFC 3261. Otherwise, if the request is syntactically correct and well structured, the agent MUST send a 200 response. If the application needs to reject the information it received, that has to be done at the application level, by triggering a new INFO request that says the previous data was not accepted.

The application information is carried in the payload of the message body. A body part associated with an Info Package is identified by a Content-Disposition header field with the value Info-Package. It can hold a single MIME type or be a multipart body that contains other body parts associated with the package, and user agents MUST support multipart body parts. A user agent MUST NOT include a message body associated with an Info Package in an INFO response, though it MAY include a body that is not associated with a package.

The Info Package mechanism does not define a delivery order mechanism. Packages can rely on the CSeq header field to detect an INFO request received out of order, and if an application needs more, that is specified as part of the associated package.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender names the package in the request, and the receiver either accepts it with a 200 response or rejects it with 469 if it never agreed to that package. A rejection of this kind does not end the call. The content itself travels in the message body, marked with a content disposition of Info-Package.

sections.title: Info Packages and User Agent Behaviour
sections.content:
A user agent that supports the Info Package mechanism MUST indicate, using the Recv-Info header field, the set of Info Packages for which it is willing to receive INFO requests for a specific session. It can list several packages in one header field, can use several header fields, and can use an empty header field. The set is provided during dialog establishment and can be updated during the invite dialog usage. The set stays valid until the agent sends a new Recv-Info header field, and once the agent has said it will accept a package and a dialog exists, it MUST be prepared to receive requests for that package until it says otherwise.

For a specific dialog usage, an agent MUST NOT send an INFO request for an Info Package until it has received an indication that the remote agent is willing to receive requests for that package, or after it has received an indication that the remote agent is no longer willing to receive them. When a remote agent sends a new set of packages, it might send an INFO request based on the old set in the meantime, in which case the receiver rejects it with a 469 response. If an agent indicates several packages that provide similar functionality, there is no way to indicate a priority order among them or that only one should be used; that is left to the application logic.

For backward compatibility, an agent that indicates support of the INFO method in the Allow header field does not implicitly indicate support of the Info Package mechanism: the Recv-Info header field is required for that, and the Allow header is still used to indicate support of the method itself.

The rules for including Recv-Info are specific. The sender of an initial INVITE request MUST include a Recv-Info header field, even if it is not willing to receive requests for any package. The receiver of a request that contains a Recv-Info header field MUST include one in a reliable 18x or 2xx response, even if the request contained an empty field and even if the receiver's set has not changed. An agent MUST NOT include a Recv-Info header field in a response if the associated request did not contain one. In contrast to the rules for session description answers, the receiver is not restricted to generating its own set as a subset of the set it received. The receiver may include the same Recv-Info value in several responses for the same transaction, but it MUST use the same value in all responses for that transaction.

There are also fallback rules. If the receiver of a request that contains a Recv-Info header field rejects the request, both sender and receiver MUST roll back to the set of packages used before the request was sent, and the same applies when the receiver of an INVITE or re-INVITE has included Recv-Info in a provisional response but later rejects the request.

A user agent may insert a Recv-Info header field in a REGISTER request, but it SHALL NOT include a header value for a specific package unless that package's specification says how the registrar should interpret and use the value, for example to determine request targets. More appropriate mechanisms, such as those in RFC 3840, are recommended instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side states, in a header field, which kinds of package it will accept for this call, and can change that list later. A request for a package the other side never agreed to is refused. If a call setup fails, both sides go back to the list they had before.

sections.title: Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax extensions to the ABNF of RFC 3261 needed for the INFO method, and the definitions of the Info-Package and Recv-Info header fields, are given in Augmented Backus-Naur Form conformant to RFC 5234. The method is added to the Method production, and the two header fields are added to the message-header production. The Info-Package header field carries an Info-package-type, which is an Info-package-name followed by any number of Info-package-param values, where the name is a token and the parameters are generic parameters. The Recv-Info header field carries an optional list of Info-package-type values separated by commas.

When matching the Info Package types listed in Recv-Info with the one in the Info-Package header field, the name portion is compared octet by octet, so the Info Package name is case sensitive, and the parameters are not part of the comparison. This document does not define values for Info Package types; individual package specifications define them.
sections.plainLanguage: The method and the two header fields are written out in the formal syntax used for SIP, so that a parser can be built from the document alone. The package name is compared exactly, including its case.

sections.title: Choosing Whether to Use INFO
sections.content:
This section covers the considerations to take into account when deciding whether the use of an Info Package is appropriate for a particular use case.

When designing an Info Package it is important to ask whether signaling with INFO requests within a SIP dialog is an appropriate mechanism, and whether it is the most reasonable choice or merely because it is easy. Choosing an inappropriate mechanism can have negative effects on the SIP networks where it is used.

INFO messages differ from many other SIP messages in carrying application information whose size and rate are determined by the application. This can cause application traffic to interfere with other traffic on the same infrastructure, or to interfere with itself when the data rate becomes too high. There is no default throttling mechanism for INFO requests, and apart from session establishment the number of SIP messages exchanged during a normal session is small. Some applications, such as those sending Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency tones, can generate a burst of up to 20 messages per second, and others, such as constant GPS location updates, generate a high rate of requests. A designer needs to consider the effect of the size and rate of the messages on the network and on other traffic, since it normally cannot be ensured that INFO messages travel over a congestion-controlled transport end to end.

SIP messages tend to be relatively small, on the order of 500 bytes to 32K bytes, and SIP is a poor mechanism for direct exchange of bulk data beyond these limits, especially if the headers plus body exceed the UDP MTU. Appropriate mechanisms for such traffic include HTTP, MSRP, or other media plane data transport mechanisms.

The RFC then describes alternatives. For application level interaction on the signaling plane, the subscription-based events mechanism uses the SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods, in which a user agent requests state information such as keypad presses from a device or key-map images from an application server. Event Packages play the role of disambiguating the context of a message for subscription-based events, in the same way the Info Package mechanism does for application information exchange. While an INFO request is always part of an existing invite dialog usage, a SUBSCRIBE request creates a separate dialog usage and is normally sent outside an existing dialog. The subscription mechanism can also be used to receive state information about dialogs and sessions without requiring the entities to be part of the route set of those dialogs. As SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY messages traverse stateful SIP proxies and back-to-back user agents, the resource impact of the subscription dialogs, and the number of subscription dialogs per user, need to be considered. The MESSAGE method defines one-time instant message exchange, typically for sending MIME contents for rendering to the user.

For the media plane, the RFC notes that the data exchanged on a media channel does not traverse the SIP signaling intermediaries, so when a lot of information is exchanged and the intermediaries have no need to examine it, a media plane mechanism is recommended. A low-latency requirement is one strong indicator, since exchanging information through the SIP routing network can introduce hundreds of milliseconds of latency. The Media Resource Control Protocol is one such mechanism, where a connection-oriented channel such as TCP or SCTP is established, and MSRP defines session-based instant messaging as well as bulk file transfer. A SIP-independent mechanism such as HTTP is another option, where the user agent knows a rendezvous point to which it can direct HTTP requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The method is for application data, so an application that sends a lot of it can overload the signaling network. The RFC lists what else to use instead: subscriptions for state information, a media channel for anything large or latency-sensitive, and plain HTTP for anything outside SIP.

sections.title: What an Info Package Specification Must Cover
sections.content:
An Info Package specification defines the content and semantics of the information carried in an INFO message associated with the package. If a package needs to extend or modify the behaviour described in this document, that behaviour MUST be described in the package specification, and it is bad practice for a package specification to repeat the procedures defined here unless it is needed for clarity or emphasis. Package specifications MUST NOT weaken any behaviour designated with SHOULD or MUST, though they MAY strengthen SHOULD, MAY or RECOMMENDED requirements to MUST if the applications require it. Each specification MUST address the issues in the subsections that follow, or document why an issue does not apply to it.

The specification MUST contain an overall description: what type of information is carried in INFO requests associated with the package, and for what types of applications and functionalities user agents can use it. If the package is defined for a specific application, the specification MUST state which applications can use it.

It MUST describe why the Info Package mechanism, rather than some other mechanism, was chosen for the use case. Common reasons are a requirement for SIP proxies or back-to-back user agents to see the transported application information, which would not be the case if the information travelled on a media path, or that it is not seen as feasible to establish separate dialogs in order to transport the information.

It MUST define an Info Package name, used as a header field value such as infoX, conforming to the ABNF in Section 9.2. The mechanism does not support package versioning; specific message body payloads can contain version information handled by the applications, and even a name containing version numbering does not make the mechanism distinguish a version number from the rest of the name.

The specification MAY define Info Package parameters used in the Recv-Info or Info-Package header fields, and MUST define their syntax and semantics and say whether a parameter applies to Recv-Info, to Info-Package or to both. By default a parameter applies only to the package for which it was defined, and while parameters of different packages may share a name, their semantics are specific to the package, so it is RECOMMENDED not to reuse a name whose semantics differ.

The specification MAY define SIP option-tags, whose registration requirements are in RFC 5727. It MUST define which message body part MIME types are associated with the package, either by defining them or by referring to other documents, and if several MIME types are associated it MUST say whether user agents need to use multipart body parts to include several in one request. It MUST document any restrictions on use, such as whether user agents may send overlapping outstanding requests for the package or have to wait for the response to a previous one, and whether they must support other SIP extensions when using the package. Because the SIP stack may not know about package-specific restrictions, the application logic has to handle the case where user agents do not follow them.

If there is a maximum or minimum rate at which requests may be sent within a dialog, the specification MUST document the rate values, and MAY define parameters for negotiating them. If the application information requires a certain level of security, the specification MUST describe the mechanisms user agents need to use, or state that no additional security beyond the underlying SIP protocol is required. It is strongly RECOMMENDED that the specification define implementation details, or refer to another location, so that several implementations can support the package, and it is RECOMMENDED that it provide demonstrative message flow diagrams paired with complete messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says exactly what a package specification has to contain: what the data is, why this method was chosen, what it is called, what shape the data has, how often it may be sent, and how it is protected. The rules here cannot be weakened by a package, only tightened.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
By eliminating multiple usages of INFO messages without adequate community review, and by eliminating the possibility of rogue user agents confusing another agent by purposely sending unrelated INFO requests, the RFC expects this clarification of the use of INFO to improve the security of the Internet. While rogue agents can still send unrelated INFO requests, the mechanism enables the receiving agent and other security devices to associate INFO requests with the Info Packages that were negotiated for the session.

If the content of an Info Package payload is private, user agents will need to use end-to-end encryption such as S/MIME to prevent access to it. This matters because the transport of INFO is likely not to be end to end, but to pass through SIP proxies and back-to-back user agents that the user may not trust.

The INFO request transports application level information, and one implication is that INFO messages may require a higher level of protection than the underlying SIP dialog signaling. If the SIP signaling is not protected from eavesdropping or from authentication and repudiation attacks, for example by using TLS transport, then the INFO request and its contents are vulnerable as well. Even with SIP over TLS, any SIP hop along the path may be a security concern. The Info Package mechanism itself does not define a SIP option-tag, but an individual package specification can define one.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the messages travel through proxies that may not be trusted, private content has to be protected from end to end, and the signalling underneath has to be protected too. Naming the packages also helps, because a receiver can check that a request belongs to something the session agreed on.

THE ABNF OF THE METHOD AND THE TWO HEADER FIELDS, FROM RFC 6086 SECTION 9.2

data.title: INFO syntax
data.code:
INFOm               = %x49.4E.46.4F ; INFO in caps
Method              =/ INFOm

message-header      =/ (Info-Package / Recv-Info) CRLF
Info-Package        =  "Info-Package" HCOLON Info-package-type
Recv-Info           =  "Recv-Info" HCOLON [Info-package-list]
Info-package-list   =  Info-package-type *( COMMA Info-package-type )
Info-package-type   =  Info-package-name *( SEMI Info-package-param )
Info-package-name   =  token
Info-package-param  =  generic-param

items.title: Overall description
items.text: What kind of information the package carries and what applications can use it.

items.title: Applicability
items.text: Why the Info Package mechanism was chosen rather than another one.

items.title: Name
items.text: The token used in the Recv-Info and Info-Package header fields. The name is case sensitive.

items.title: Parameters
items.text: Any parameters, their syntax, their meaning, and which header field they apply to.

items.title: Body parts
items.text: Which MIME types belong to the package, and whether multipart is needed.

items.title: Usage restrictions
items.text: Whether requests may overlap, and what other extensions are required.

items.title: Rate
items.text: Any maximum or minimum rate at which requests may be sent.

items.title: Security
items.text: The mechanisms needed, or a statement that plain SIP security is enough.
